intro:
## Part 1: General Introduction

### Outline of Ezekiel

1. Yahweh calls Ezekiel to speak his words (1:1–3:27)
2. Yahweh judges Judah and Jerusalem (4:1–24:27)
3. Ezekiel prophesies against nearby nations (25:1–32:32)
4. Yahweh explains the fall of Jerusalem (33:1–33)
5. Ezekiel brings messages of hope (34:1–48:35)
  A. A new shepherd (34:1–31)
  B. Edom destroyed (35:1–15)
  C. Israel restored (36:1–37:28)
  D. Gog and Magog (38:1–39:29)
  E. Jerusalem and the temple restored (40:1–48:35)

### What is Ezekiel about?

The book of Ezekiel contains messages that Ezekiel prophesied between 593 B.C. and 571 B.C. The Jewish people, including Ezekiel, were exiled in Babylonia. Ezekiel told them that God was punishing them because they had sinned against him. He also said that God was going to further punish them by destroying Jerusalem and his temple. This happened in 586 B.C. After that, God gave Ezekiel messages that assured the people that God would restore them to their land. He said that God was using Babylon to punish them, but that eventually another nation would defeat the Babylonians. Ezekiel also prophesied about how God would restore Jerusalem and the temple so that the people could worship and sacrifice to him again. Ezekiel then described how the land would be divided again among the tribes of Israel.

### How should the title of this book be translated?

“Ezekiel” or “The Book of Ezekiel” is the traditional name for this book. Translators may also call it “The Messages from God Brought by Ezekiel.”

### Who wrote the book of Ezekiel?

Ezekiel wrote the prophecies in the book of Ezekiel. He was a prophet and priest who lived near Babylon in the time of the exile.

## Part 2: Important Religious and Cultural Concepts

### What was Ezekiel’s temple?

Several chapters of the book of Ezekiel give a detailed description of a new temple that Ezekiel sees in a vision. However, the temple that the people built after going back to Jerusalem was much smaller. Because Ezekiel’s temple has never been built, some scholars think that this temple is to be built in the future. Others think that it is a description of the heavenly, ideal temple. Other scholars think that Ezekiel’s temple is symbolic of the Church.

### Do the sacrifices in Ezekiel follow the law of Moses?

The sacrifices in Ezekiel 46 are somewhat different than the required sacrifices in Numbers 28. This may be because Ezekiel prophesied about a new temple with new sacrifices.

chapters.1:
## Structure and Formatting

1. Ezekiel sees Yahweh’s glorious appearance (1–14)
2. Ezekiel sees the living creatures and heavenly wheels (15–21)
3. Ezekiel sees the glory of Yahweh above the throne (22–28)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The exile

Ezekiel prophesied in Babylonia. When he mentions living “among the exiles,” he means he was one of the Israelite people whom the Babylonians had forcibly removed from the land of Judah. He begins the book describing visions he saw five years after the exile of King Jehoiachin.
chapters.2:
## Structure and Formatting

1. Yahweh calls Ezekiel to speak to rebellious Israel (1–5)
2. Yahweh strengthens Ezekiel against their opposition (6–8)
3. Yahweh gives Ezekiel his words to proclaim (9–10)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### A house of rebellion

Yahweh repeatedly calls Israel “a house of rebellion,” picturing the people as a household marked by refusal to obey him.
chapters.3:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter completes the commissioning of Ezekiel that began in chapter 2, and it ends with the prophet confined to his house and unable to speak unless Yahweh gives him a message.

1. Yahweh commissions Ezekiel as a watchman (1–11)
2. Yahweh’s Spirit strengthens and guides Ezekiel (12–15)
3. Yahweh holds Ezekiel responsible for warning the wicked (16–21)
4. Yahweh reveals his glory and commands Ezekiel to speak (22–27)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Eating the scroll

Yahweh commands Ezekiel to eat a scroll, and it tastes as sweet as honey. This symbolic act represents the prophet taking Yahweh’s message into himself, so that the words he speaks are Yahweh’s words and not his own.

### The prophet as a watchman

A watchman guarded an ancient city by looking out for danger and warning the people. In the same way, Ezekiel must warn the people of Yahweh’s judgment, and Yahweh holds him accountable for the death of anyone whom he fails to warn.
chapters.4:
## Structure and Formatting

Yahweh commands Ezekiel to perform a series of symbolic actions that portray the coming siege of Jerusalem and the famine that will accompany it.

1. Yahweh commands Ezekiel to portray Jerusalem’s siege (1–3)
2. Ezekiel bears Israel’s guilt and judgment (4–8)
3. Ezekiel portrays the famine and suffering of Jerusalem (9–17)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Symbolic actions

Ezekiel does not merely announce the siege of Jerusalem; he acts it out with a brick, an iron griddle, and his own body. Such enacted signs were a recognized form of prophecy and were understood to portray what Yahweh was about to do.

### Bearing iniquity

When Ezekiel “carries the iniquity” of Israel and of Judah, he is not being punished for his own sin. He is publicly representing the guilt of the people and the punishment that it deserves.

### Unclean food

The law of Moses forbade certain foods and required that food be prepared in ways that kept a person ritually pure. Baking bread over human excrement would defile both the food and the prophet, which is why Ezekiel protests in verse 14.
chapters.5:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter completes the series of symbolic actions that began in chapter 4 and then interprets them.

1. Yahweh judges Jerusalem for its rebellion (1–4)
2. Yahweh declares judgment because of Jerusalem’s abominations (5–10)
3. Yahweh brings famine, death, and scattering upon Jerusalem (11–17)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Symbolic actions

Ezekiel acts out the coming judgment rather than only announcing it. Shaving the head and beard was in itself a sign of mourning and humiliation, and each portion of the hair stands for a group of the people, as Yahweh explains in verse 12.

### Defiling the sanctuary

Yahweh gives as a reason for this judgment that the people have brought detestable things into his temple. To make the sanctuary unclean was to treat as common the one place that Yahweh had set apart for himself.

### The curses of the covenant

Famine, the sword, plague, wild animals, and parents eating their own children are the very punishments that Yahweh had warned of in the law of Moses if his people broke the covenant. The first hearers would have recognized these disasters as covenant curses rather than as random calamities.
chapters.6:
## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter Yahweh tells Ezekiel to prophesy against the mountains of Israel, where the people worshiped idols.

1. Judgment on the places of idol worship (1–7)
    1. Yahweh commands Ezekiel to speak to the mountains of Israel (1–3)
    2. Yahweh will destroy the altars and leave the dead lying in front of the idols (4–7)
2. Some people will survive and remember Yahweh in exile (8–10)
3. Ezekiel is to lament over Israel’s coming destruction (11–14)
    1. The people will die by sword, famine, and plague (11–12)
    2. The dead will lie among the idols, and the land will become desolate (13–14)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### High places

The high places were hilltop sites where the Israelites built altars and set up idols to worship. Yahweh addresses the mountains, hills, stream beds, and valleys because that is where this idol worship took place, and he will defile those sites with the bodies of the people who worshiped there.

### Idolatry as prostitution

In 6:9 Yahweh speaks of the people’s idol worship as if it were prostitution, that is, sexual unfaithfulness to him. This comparison appears often in Ezekiel.
chapters.7:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is a prophecy in poetic language announcing that the end has come for the land of Israel.

1. Yahweh tells Ezekiel to announce the end of the land of Israel (1–4)
2. The day of judgment is coming (5–13)
    1. The end has come because of the people’s ways (5–9)
    2. The day has arrived, and buying and selling will no longer matter (10–13)
3. The people will be helpless and will mourn (14–18)
4. Their wealth will not save them, and foreigners will defile Yahweh’s temple (19–22)
5. Yahweh will bring the nations, and no leader will be able to help (23–27)

Some translations set lines of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 7:2–27.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The day of Yahweh

Throughout this chapter, “the end,” “the time,” and “the day” refer to the time when Yahweh will punish the people of Israel for their sins.

### Mourning practices

In this culture, people expressed grief by wearing sackcloth and shaving their heads (v. 18). Ezekiel uses these practices to show how the people will mourn when Yahweh judges them.

### Ritual uncleanness

In verses 19–20, Yahweh compares the people’s silver and gold to the impurity of menstruation. Under the law of Moses, menstruation made a person ritually unclean as well as physically unclean, so the comparison shows that the people will regard their wealth as something that kept them from God and therefore as something detestable to be thrown away.
chapters.8:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter begins a vision that continues through chapter 11. Yahweh takes Ezekiel to the temple in Jerusalem and shows him a series of increasingly serious abominations that the people are committing there.

1. Ezekiel is carried in a vision from his house to Jerusalem (1–4)
2. Yahweh shows Ezekiel abominations in the temple (5–16)
    1. The image of jealousy north of the altar gate (5–6)
    2. Seventy elders burning incense to carved images (7–13)
    3. Women weeping for Tammuz (14–15)
    4. Twenty-five men worshiping the sun (16)
3. Yahweh says that he will punish them without pity (17–18)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Ezekiel’s vision of Jerusalem

Ezekiel was living among the exiles in Babylonia. He did not travel to Jerusalem physically; he saw the temple and what was happening there in a vision from God (v. 3).

### Idolatry in the temple

The temple was the place where the people were to worship only Yahweh, but the people of Judah were worshiping images of false gods there. For example, the “image of jealousy” was an idol that provoked Yahweh to be jealous (v. 3). Tammuz was a god of the Babylonians and other peoples, for whom women performed ritual weeping (v. 14). The men in verse 16 turned their backs on the temple to bow down to the sun.
chapters.9:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the vision that began in chapter 8. Yahweh responds to the abominations that he showed Ezekiel in the temple by sending agents to punish Jerusalem.

1. Yahweh summons six executioners and a man clothed in linen (1–2)
2. Yahweh commands the man to mark the faithful and the others to kill everyone else (3–7)
3. Ezekiel pleads for the remnant, and Yahweh answers that he will not spare them (8–10)
4. The man clothed in linen reports that he has done what Yahweh commanded (11)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The glory of God leaving the cherub

In 9:3, the glory of God moves from above the cherubs to the threshold of the temple. These cherubs would be the ones on the top of the ark of the covenant in the innermost sanctuary (Holy of Holies) in the temple. This is the first stage of a movement that continues in chapters 10 and 11, where God’s glory leaves the temple and then the city.

### The mark on the foreheads

The man clothed in linen puts a mark on the people who grieve over the abomination in the city, and the executioners must not harm anyone who has this mark. The mark identifies these people so that they will be protected, because they are true worshipers of Yahweh. The text does not say what the mark looked like, so a general word for “mark” is best.

### Judgment beginning at the sanctuary

Yahweh tells the executioners to begin at his sanctuary and to fill its courts with dead bodies. Dead bodies made a place ritually unclean, so this command shows that, because of the people’s sin, Yahweh was no longer treating the temple as holy.
chapters.10:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the vision that began in Ezekiel 8. The man clothed in linen carries out Yahweh’s command to scatter burning coals over Jerusalem, and the glory of Yahweh moves farther away from the temple.

1. Yahweh commands the man clothed in linen to take burning coals from among the cherubs (1–8)
    1. Yahweh gives the command (1–2)
    2. The cloud and the glory of Yahweh fill the temple and its courtyard (3–5)
    3. A cherub gives fire to the man (6–8)
2. Ezekiel describes the cherubs and their wheels (9–17)
3. The glory of Yahweh leaves the threshold and stops at the east gate (18–19)
4. Ezekiel recognizes these cherubs as the beings that he saw by the river of Kebar (20–22)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The glory of Yahweh leaving the temple

The glory of Yahweh moved to the threshold of the temple in 9:3. In this chapter it moves again to the threshold (v. 4), then rests over the cherubs at the east gate (vv. 18–19). It leaves the city completely in 11:23. This shows that Yahweh was abandoning the temple because of the people’s sin.

### The cherubs and the wheels

The beings and wheels in this chapter are the same ones that Ezekiel saw in chapter 1, where he called them “beings.” Here he says that he realized they were cherubs (v. 20). Translators may want to use the same words for the faces, wings, wheels, and eyes as in chapter 1.
chapters.11:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter concludes the vision that began in Ezekiel 8:1, in which the Spirit carries Ezekiel to Jerusalem and shows him the sins of its people and Yahweh’s judgment on them.

1. Yahweh condemns the leaders of Jerusalem (1–13)
    1. Ezekiel sees 25 men at the east gate of the temple (1–4)
    2. Ezekiel prophesies against them (5–12)
    3. Pelatiah dies, and Ezekiel cries out to Yahweh (13)
2. Yahweh promises to restore the exiles (14–21)
3. The glory of Yahweh leaves the city, and Ezekiel returns to the exiles (22–25)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The departure of Yahweh’s glory

In 11:22–23, the glory of Yahweh rises with the cherubs and leaves Jerusalem, stopping on the mountain east of the city. This completes the departure that began in chapters 9 and 10 and shows that Yahweh has abandoned the city to judgment.

### Yahweh’s presence with the exiles

The people who remained in Jerusalem claimed that the land belonged to them because the exiles were far from Yahweh. Yahweh answers that he himself has been a sanctuary for the exiles and that he will bring them back and give them a new heart and a new spirit so that they will obey him.
chapters.12:
## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, Yahweh has Ezekiel perform two more symbolic actions that warn the people of Jerusalem about the coming exile, and then he answers sayings that claimed Ezekiel’s prophecies would never come true.

1. The sign of going into exile (1–16)
    1. Yahweh commands Ezekiel to act out going into exile (1–6)
    2. Ezekiel performs the sign (7)
    3. Yahweh explains that the sign shows what will happen to the prince and the people of Jerusalem (8–16)
2. The sign of eating and drinking with trembling (17–20)
3. Yahweh rejects the proverb that visions never come true (21–25)
4. Yahweh declares that his words will be fulfilled without delay (26–28)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Symbolic actions

Ezekiel packs a bag like someone going into exile, digs through a wall, and eats and drinks while trembling. These actions are a sign that shows the people what is about to happen to them. Translators should describe these actions plainly so that readers can picture what Ezekiel did.

### The prince

The “prince” in Jerusalem (10, 12) is King Zedekiah. What Yahweh says about him in verses 12–13 happened when he fled Jerusalem by night, was captured, was blinded, and was taken to Babylon, where he died (see 2 Kings 25:4–7). That is why Yahweh says he will be brought to Babylon but will not see it.
chapters.13:
## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, Yahweh tells Ezekiel to prophesy against Israelites who claim to speak for Yahweh but whom Yahweh has not sent.

1. Yahweh condemns the prophets who prophesy from their own hearts (1–9)
2. Yahweh will tear down the plastered wall of their false message of peace (10–16)
3. Yahweh condemns the women who prophesy falsely and trap people with magic (17–19)
4. Yahweh will rescue his people from these women (20–23)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 13:9.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### False prophets

The people Ezekiel condemns in this chapter claimed that their visions and messages came from Yahweh, but they invented them. They told the people that there would be peace, even though Yahweh had said that he would judge Jerusalem.

### Magic bands and veils

The women in 13:17–23 used objects such as bands sewn on the wrists and coverings for the head to practice magic and divination. The exact nature of these objects is unknown, so your translation can use general terms for them.
chapters.14:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter contains two messages from Yahweh. The first answers some elders who came to inquire of Yahweh while they continued to worship idols. The second explains that the presence of a few righteous people would not save Jerusalem from Yahweh’s judgment.

1. Yahweh refuses to be consulted by elders who worship idols (1–5)
2. Yahweh calls Israel to repent and warns idolaters and the prophets who answer them (6–11)
3. Not even Noah, Daniel, and Job could rescue anyone but themselves (12–20)
4. Yahweh will send his four judgments on Jerusalem, and the survivors will show that he acted justly (21–23)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Inquiring of Yahweh through a prophet

Israelites who wanted guidance from Yahweh would go to a prophet and ask him to inquire of Yahweh on their behalf. Yahweh says that he will not give an ordinary answer to people who come to him in this way while they are devoted to idols, but he will answer them with judgment.

### Noah, Daniel, and Job

The Israelites regarded these three men as outstanding examples of righteous people. Yahweh names them to show that even the most righteous people could save only their own lives, not their children or their land. Some scholars think that this Daniel is the Daniel of the book of Daniel, who lived at the same time as Ezekiel, while others think that he is an ancient righteous man known from other stories.

### The four judgments

Sword, famine, dangerous wild animals, and plague were the punishments that Yahweh had warned in the law of Moses that he would send on Israel if they were unfaithful to him.
chapters.15:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is a short parable about the wood of a grapevine, followed by Yahweh’s explanation of what it means for the people of Jerusalem.

1. The parable of the useless vine wood (1–5)
2. Yahweh explains the parable (6–8)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The vine as a picture of Israel

Other parts of the Bible often picture Israel as a vine that Yahweh planted and expected to bear fruit. Here, however, Yahweh speaks only of the vine’s wood (small branches which people prune off), which people cannot use to make anything, so they use it only as fuel. The point is that the people of Jerusalem are as useless to Yahweh as vine wood, and he will destroy them.

### Fire as a picture of judgment

In the parable, fire burns the vine wood. When Yahweh explains the parable, fire represents the disasters he sends on Jerusalem. The people had survived earlier attacks by the Babylonians, but the coming judgment will completely destroy them.
chapters.16:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is an extended allegory in which Yahweh describes Jerusalem as an abandoned baby girl whom he rescued and married, but who became an unfaithful wife.

1. Yahweh tells Ezekiel to confront Jerusalem with her abominations (1–2)
2. Yahweh rescues Jerusalem as an abandoned baby, marries her, and makes her beautiful (3–14)
3. Jerusalem acts like a prostitute (15–34)
    1. She uses Yahweh’s gifts to worship idols and sacrifices her children (15–22)
    2. She builds shrines everywhere and seeks lovers among the nations (23–34)
4. Yahweh will punish Jerusalem as an adulterous wife (35–43)
5. Jerusalem is worse than her sisters Samaria and Sodom (44–58)
6. Yahweh promises to remember his covenant and establish an everlasting covenant (59–63)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Prostitution and adultery as unfaithfulness to Yahweh

Yahweh’s covenant with Israel is pictured as a marriage. Worshiping other gods and relying on foreign nations such as Egypt, Assyria, and Babylon instead of Yahweh is described as prostitution and adultery.

### Child sacrifice

Some of the people of Jerusalem sacrificed their children to idols by burning them. The chapter refers to this as making them “pass through” the fire to the idols.

### Sisters Samaria and Sodom

Yahweh calls Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom, and Sodom, the city that he destroyed long before, Jerusalem’s sisters. They are like Jerusalem because they also sinned, but Yahweh says that Jerusalem sinned even more than they did.
chapters.17:
## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter Yahweh gives Ezekiel a parable about two eagles and a vine, explains what it means, and then promises to plant a new cedar.

1. Yahweh tells Ezekiel to speak a parable to Israel (1–2)
2. The parable of the two eagles and the vine (3–10)
    1. The first eagle plants a vine (3–6)
    2. The vine turns toward a second eagle (7–8)
    3. The vine will wither (9–10)
3. Yahweh explains the parable (11–21)
    1. The king of Babylon makes a covenant with a new king of Judah (11–14)
    2. The king of Judah rebels and will die in Babylon (15–18)
    3. Yahweh will punish him for breaking the oath he made in Yahweh’s name (19–21)
4. Yahweh will plant a tender shoot on a high mountain of Israel (22–24)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 17:3–10.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Zedekiah’s covenant with the king of Babylon

Nebuchadnezzar, the king of Babylon, took King Jehoiachin to Babylon and made Zedekiah king of Judah after Zedekiah swore an oath of loyalty to him. Zedekiah later asked Egypt for help. Because Zedekiah swore that oath in Yahweh’s name, Yahweh calls it “my oath” and “my covenant” in 17:19.

### The tender shoot

In 17:22–24, the tender shoot that Yahweh plants represents a future king from David’s family whom Yahweh will establish, and the birds that live under it represent people from many nations who find protection in his kingdom.
chapters.18:
## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Inherited Guilt

God does not punish children for the sins of their parents, but only punishes them for their own sins. Despite this, the parents’ sins may still have consequences for their children.
chapters.19:
## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Judah destroyed

The first king was taken as a captive to Egypt, the next was taken as a captive to Babylon. Now Judah is not prospering.
chapters.20:
## Structure and Formatting

Yahweh refuses to let the elders of Israel inquire of him and instead has Ezekiel recount Israel’s long history of rebellion, followed by a promise of judgment and restoration.

1. The elders come to inquire of Yahweh, and he refuses them (1–4)
2. Yahweh recounts Israel’s rebellion against him (5–29)
    1. In Egypt (5–9)
    2. The first generation in the wilderness (10–17)
    3. The second generation in the wilderness (18–26)
    4. In the land Yahweh gave them (27–29)
3. Yahweh condemns the idolatry of the present generation (30–32)
4. Yahweh promises to judge his people and bring them back to their land (33–44)
5. Yahweh’s message against the forest of the south (45–49)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Acting for the sake of his name

Yahweh repeatedly holds back his punishment so that his name, meaning his reputation, would not be profaned among the nations who had seen him rescue Israel from Egypt.

### Sabbaths and idols

The chapter presents keeping Yahweh’s Sabbaths as a sign of his relationship with Israel, and worshiping idols at the high places as breaking that relationship.  Verses 26 and 31 refer to the practice of sacrificing children to idols.
chapters.21:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is a series of oracles about the sword that Yahweh sends in judgment, first against Jerusalem and the land of Israel and then against the Ammonites.

1. Yahweh draws his sword against Jerusalem and the land of Israel (1–7)
    1. The sword comes out of its sheath (1–5)
    2. Ezekiel groans as a sign of the coming disaster (6–7)
2. The song of the sword (8–17)
3. The king of Babylon chooses the road to Jerusalem (18–27)
    1. The king uses divination at the fork in the road (18–23)
    2. Yahweh announces judgment on Jerusalem and its prince (24–27)
4. The sword against the Ammonites (28–32)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 21:9–17.

The ULT follows the verse numbering of most English translations. In the Hebrew text, verses 1–32 of this chapter are numbered 21:6–37, because the Hebrew chapter begins with the verses that the ULT numbers as 20:45–49.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The sword of Yahweh

The  in this chapter represents the army of  that Yahweh sends to punish his people and the people of . Yahweh speaks of it as his own sword to show that he is the one bringing this judgment.

### Divination

In verses 21–22, the king of Babylon uses three kinds of  to decide which city to attack: shaking arrows, consulting household idols, and examining the liver of a sacrificed animal. Yahweh controls even these pagan practices so that the king goes to Jerusalem.
chapters.22:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter contains three messages from Yahweh that list the sins of Jerusalem and of all Israel and announce his judgment on them.

1. Yahweh accuses Jerusalem, the city of blood (1–16)
    1. Jerusalem’s bloodshed and idols make her guilty and unclean (1–5)
    2. Yahweh lists the sins committed in the city (6–12)
    3. Yahweh will scatter the people among the nations (13–16)
2. Yahweh will melt Israel like metal in a furnace (17–22)
3. All the leaders and people of the land are guilty (23–31)
    1. Prophets, priests, princes, and people have all sinned (23–29)
    2. No one stands in the gap, so Yahweh pours out his wrath (30–31)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The city of blood

Yahweh calls Jerusalem “the city of blood” because many people were murdered there and the leaders used violence to gain wealth. See .

### Refining metal

In verses 18–22, Yahweh compares Israel to the worthless material left over when silver is melted in a . Just as a metalworker melts metal with fire, Yahweh will gather his people into Jerusalem and punish them there.

### Holy and common

The priests were supposed to teach the people the difference between what was  and what was common, and between what was clean and unclean. Instead, they profaned Yahweh’s holy things and ignored his Sabbaths, so that Yahweh himself was profaned among them (verse 26). See .
chapters.23:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is an extended allegory in which Yahweh describes Samaria and Jerusalem as two sisters who became his wives and then were unfaithful to him.

1. Two sisters, Oholah and Oholibah, prostitute themselves in Egypt and become Yahweh’s wives (1–4)
2. Oholah (Samaria) lusts after the Assyrians and is punished by them (5–10)
3. Oholibah (Jerusalem) becomes even more corrupt than her sister (11–21)
    1. She lusts after the Assyrians (11–13)
    2. She lusts after the Babylonians and then turns away from them (14–18)
    3. She returns to the prostitution of her youth in Egypt (19–21)
4. Yahweh announces his judgment on Oholibah (22–35)
    1. Her former lovers will attack and humiliate her (22–27)
    2. Yahweh will give her into the hands of those she hates (28–31)
    3. She will drink the cup of her sister (32–34)
    4. She will bear the consequences of forgetting Yahweh (35)
5. Yahweh accuses and judges both sisters (36–49)
    1. They committed adultery, sacrificed their children, and defiled Yahweh’s sanctuary (36–42)
    2. Righteous men will judge them as adulteresses and murderers (43–45)
    3. An assembly will stone them and destroy their houses (46–49)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Prostitution as unfaithfulness to Yahweh

Yahweh pictures his covenant with Israel as a marriage. When Samaria and Jerusalem worshiped idols and trusted in foreign nations such as Egypt, Assyria, and Babylon, it was like a wife committing  or acting as a . See  and .

### The cup of judgment

In verses 31–34, Yahweh speaks of the punishment he will give Jerusalem as a cup that she must drink. The cup is the same punishment that Samaria received, and drinking it will make Jerusalem like a drunken person who suffers horror and desolation.

### Child sacrifice

In verses 37–39, Yahweh accuses the two sisters of killing their children as sacrifices to idols and then coming into his  on the same day, which profaned it. See .
chapters.24:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter contains Ezekiel’s last messages of judgment against Jerusalem before the city falls, dated to the day the Babylonian army began its siege of the city.

1. Yahweh tells Ezekiel to record the date the siege of Jerusalem began (1–2)
2. The parable of the cooking pot (3–14)
    1. The pot is filled with choice meat and boiled (3–5)
    2. Woe to the city of bloodshed, which is like a rusted pot (6–8)
    3. Yahweh will heat the empty pot until its rust burns away (9–12)
    4. Yahweh will not relent in punishing Jerusalem (13–14)
3. The death of Ezekiel’s wife is a sign to the people (15–24)
    1. Yahweh forbids Ezekiel to mourn for his wife (15–18)
    2. Ezekiel explains what his actions mean for the people (19–24)
4. Ezekiel will no longer be mute when a survivor brings news from Jerusalem (25–27)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 24:3–12.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Uncovered blood

The law of Moses required people to cover with dust the blood of animals they killed, and blood left uncovered on a bare rock was thought to call out for vengeance. In 24:7–8, Jerusalem has shed blood openly, so Yahweh leaves that blood exposed as a witness against the city.

### Mourning customs

In this culture, people mourned by removing their turbans and sandals, covering the lower part of their faces, and eating food that neighbors brought to them. Yahweh forbids Ezekiel to do any of these things to show that the people will be too overwhelmed by the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple to mourn properly.
chapters.25:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter begins a series of prophecies against the nations around Israel that continues through chapter 32. It contains four short judgment speeches, each against a neighbor that treated Judah’s fall with scorn.

1. Judgment on Ammon (1–7)
    1. Ammon said “Aha!” over the temple, the land, and the exiles (1–5)
    2. Ammon rejoiced with contempt over the land of Israel (6–7)
2. Judgment on Moab (8–11)
3. Judgment on Edom (12–14)
4. Judgment on Philistia (15–17)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Yahweh’s judgment on nations that scorned Judah

Ammon, Moab, Edom, and the Philistines each mocked Judah or took revenge on it when Babylon destroyed the temple and sent the people into exile. Yahweh treats this as an offense against himself and his people, and he declares that he will punish them.

### “You will know that I am Yahweh”

Most of these prophecies end by saying that the punished nation will know that “I am Yahweh.” This shows that the purpose of the judgment is for these nations to recognize Yahweh’s power and authority.
chapters.26:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter begins a series of prophecies against the city of Tyre that continues through 28:19. It contains four messages from Yahweh, each beginning with “thus says the Lord Yahweh.”

1. Yahweh will judge Tyre because it rejoiced over the fall of Jerusalem (1–6)
2. Nebuchadnezzar will besiege and destroy Tyre (7–14)
3. The rulers of the coastlands will mourn over Tyre (15–18)
    1. The princes of the sea mourn (15–16)
    2. The princes sing a lament over Tyre (17–18)
4. Yahweh will bring Tyre down to the pit (19–21)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 26:17–18.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Tyre

Tyre was a wealthy Phoenician trading city built on a rocky island just off the coast, with towns that depended on it on the mainland. Other peoples who traded by sea relied on it, so its fall would shock all of the coastlands.

### Mourning for a fallen city

The princes of the sea take off their fine robes, sit on the ground, and sing a funeral song over Tyre. These were common ways to show great grief.

### The pit

In verses 19–21, Yahweh speaks of Tyre going down to “the pit” and “the land of the lower parts.” These expressions refer to the place of the dead and indicate that Tyre will be destroyed completely and never exist again.
chapters.27:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is a funeral song (lament) over the city of Tyre. It continues the prophecies against Tyre that began in chapter 26. Most of the song describes Tyre as a magnificent trading ship that sinks in the middle of the sea.

1. Yahweh tells Ezekiel to sing a lament over Tyre (1–3)
2. Tyre is pictured as a beautiful ship (4–11)
    1. The ship is built from the finest materials (4–7)
    2. Men from other cities serve as its crew and soldiers (8–11)
3. The many nations that traded with Tyre (12–25)
4. The ship is wrecked in the heart of the seas (26–27)
5. The sailors and the coastlands mourn over Tyre (28–36)
    1. The sailors weep and mourn (28–31)
    2. The sailors sing their own lament over Tyre (32–36)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 27:3–11 and 27:25–36. Verses 12–25 are a list of trading partners written as prose.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Tyre’s sea trade

Tyre was a wealthy Phoenician port whose ships carried goods among many peoples. Verses 12–25 name those peoples and the goods they traded, showing how far Tyre’s trade reached and how rich it had become.

### Mourning customs

In verses 30–31 the sailors throw dust on their heads, roll in ashes, shave their heads, and put on sackcloth. These were common ways to show great grief.
chapters.28:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter concludes the prophecies against Tyre that began in chapter 26. It then gives a short prophecy against Sidon, the neighboring Phoenician city, and ends with a promise that Yahweh will restore Israel to its land.

1. Yahweh condemns the ruler of Tyre for claiming to be a god (1–10)
    1. The ruler’s wisdom and wealth made him proud (1–5)
    2. Foreigners will kill him and bring him down to the pit (6–10)
2. A lament over the king of Tyre (11–19)
    1. The king is pictured as a cherub in Eden, the garden of God (11–15)
    2. Yahweh throws the king down and destroys him (16–19)
3. Yahweh will judge Sidon (20–24)
4. Yahweh will gather Israel and let them live safely in their land (25–26)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Eden and the cherub

In verses 12–16, the lament describes the king of Tyre as if he had been in , covered with precious stones, and as if he had been a guardian  on the holy mountain of God until he sinned and was thrown out. In addition to being about the king of Tyre, Christians have often viewed this as speaking about the fall of Satan (or Adam), translators should attempt to translate the text as it is and leave the interpretation to others.

### Dying uncircumcised

Dying while uncircumcised implied being an enemy of Yahweh and thus one would go down to “the pit,” which was the place of the dead, perhaps the “bad” part of the place of the dead. This shows that the ruler of Tyre would die like an other enemy of Yahweh.
chapters.29:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter begins a series of prophecies against Egypt that continues through chapter 32. It contains two dated messages from Yahweh. The second, given about 16 years after the first, is the latest dated prophecy in the book.

1. Yahweh will judge Pharaoh and Egypt (1–16)
    1. Pharaoh, the sea monster, will be pulled out of his rivers and left to die (1–5)
    2. Egypt failed Israel like a staff made of reed (6–7)
    3. Egypt will be desolate and its people scattered for 40 years (8–12)
    4. Yahweh will bring the Egyptians back, but only as a lowly kingdom (13–16)
2. Yahweh gives Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar (17–21)
    1. Nebuchadnezzar received no wages for his campaign against Tyre (17–18)
    2. Egypt will be his army’s wages (19–20)
    3. Yahweh will make a horn sprout for Israel (21)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Pharaoh as a sea monster

Yahweh pictures  as a great creature lying in the Nile, probably like a crocodile, which Yahweh will catch with hooks and throw out to die in the open country. Pharaoh’s claim that he made the Nile, or made himself, was a claim to be a god.

### Trusting in Egypt

The kings of Judah had relied on Egypt for help against Babylon, but Egypt failed them, like a walking stick made of  that breaks and wounds the one who leans on it. After its judgment, Egypt would never again tempt Israel to  in it instead of Yahweh.

### Wages for Nebuchadnezzar

 besieged  for many years but gained little plunder from it. Yahweh says that he will give Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar as payment, because the Babylonian army had been carrying out Yahweh’s judgment.
chapters.30:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues Ezekiel’s prophecies against Egypt. It contains two messages from Yahweh: a long announcement of the day of judgment on Egypt (1–19) and a separate, dated message about Pharaoh’s broken arms (20–26).

1. The day of Yahweh will bring the sword on Egypt and her allies (1–9)
2. Yahweh will use Nebuchadnezzar to destroy Egypt (10–12)
3. Yahweh will judge Egypt’s idols and cities (13–19)
4. Yahweh breaks Pharaoh’s arms and strengthens the king of Babylon (20–26)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The day of Yahweh

In verses 2–3, the “day” that is near is the time when Yahweh comes to judge his enemies, here Egypt and the nations allied with her.

### “They will know that I am Yahweh”

This refrain (verses 8, 19, 25, and 26) states the purpose of the judgment: Egypt will recognize that Yahweh is the true God. Translate it the same way each time.
chapters.31:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is a dated message from Yahweh to Pharaoh. It uses the fall of Assyria, pictured as a great cedar tree, as a warning that Egypt will fall in the same way.

1. Yahweh tells Ezekiel to ask Pharaoh whom he is like in his greatness (1–2)
2. Assyria was a magnificent cedar that no other tree could equal (3–9)
3. Yahweh had the cedar cut down because of its pride (10–14)
4. The cedar went down to Sheol, and the nations mourned (15–17)
5. Pharaoh will be brought down like the cedar (18)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### A great tree as a picture of a kingdom

People in the ancient Near East sometimes pictured a powerful kingdom as a huge tree. In this chapter, the birds and animals that live in the cedar and the nations in its shade represent the peoples that Assyria ruled and protected, and the other trees represent other nations and their rulers.

### Sheol and the pit

The “lower land,” “Sheol,” and “the pit” all refer to the place of the dead. The Israelites thought of it as being below the ground, so the dead “go down” to it.

### The uncircumcised

Being buried among “the uncircumcised” (verse 18) was considered a shameful fate, because the Israelites regarded uncircumcised people as unclean and outside of God’s covenant.
chapters.32:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter contains the last two of Ezekiel’s prophecies against Egypt. Each begins with a date, and both are funeral songs over Pharaoh and his people.

1. A lament over Pharaoh, king of Egypt (1–16)
    1. Yahweh will catch Pharaoh like a sea monster and leave his body for scavengers (1–6)
    2. Yahweh will darken the sky, and the nations will tremble at Egypt’s fall (7–10)
    3. The king of Babylon will destroy Egypt’s people and animals (11–16)
2. Egypt goes down to the realm of the dead (17–32)
    1. Ezekiel is to wail over Egypt and send it down to the pit (17–21)
    2. Assyria, Elam, Meshech, and Tubal already lie there (22–27)
    3. Pharaoh will lie among the uncircumcised (28)
    4. Edom, the princes of the north, and the Sidonians also lie there (29–30)
    5. Pharaoh will see them and be comforted (31–32)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Lamentation

A lament was a funeral song sung over the dead. Here Ezekiel sings it over Pharaoh before he dies, which shows that his destruction is certain.

### Sheol and the pit

In 32:17–32, the “pit,” “the lower land,” and Sheol refer to the place of the dead. Ezekiel describes it as a place where defeated nations lie together in their graves.

### The uncircumcised

The Israelites considered it shameful to be buried among people who were not circumcised or among those killed in battle. Egypt practiced circumcision, so being laid among “the uncircumcised” would have been a great disgrace for Pharaoh.
chapters.33:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter begins a new part of the book. Yahweh renews Ezekiel’s role as a watchman, news arrives that Jerusalem has fallen, and Yahweh then gives messages about the people left in the land and about the exiles.

1. Ezekiel is a watchman for Israel (1–9)
    1. The duty of a watchman (1–6)
    2. Yahweh appoints Ezekiel as a watchman (7–9)
2. Yahweh answers the people’s complaints about his justice (10–20)
    1. Yahweh wants the wicked to turn back and live (10–11)
    2. Yahweh judges people by how they are living now (12–16)
    3. Yahweh’s way is fair, but the people’s way is not (17–20)
3. A fugitive reports that Jerusalem has fallen, and Ezekiel can speak again (21–22)
4. Yahweh condemns the people living in the ruins of Israel (23–29)
5. The exiles listen to Ezekiel but do not obey him (30–33)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The watchman

In ancient Israel, a watchman stood on a city wall or tower and blew a shofar (a ram’s horn) to warn the people when an enemy army approached. Yahweh uses this image to show that Ezekiel must warn the people and that each person who hears the warning is responsible to respond to it. Yahweh first gave Ezekiel this role in 3:16–21.

### Turning back from wickedness

Verses 10–20 repeat the teaching of chapter 18. Yahweh judges each person according to whether he is now doing what is righteous or what is evil, and he wants wicked people to repent and live.

### The fall of Jerusalem

The fugitive’s report in verse 21 fulfills what Yahweh told Ezekiel in 24:26–27. Yahweh had kept Ezekiel from speaking freely since 3:26, but now he opens Ezekiel’s mouth.

### The claim to the land

The people left in Judah reasoned that since God gave the land to Abraham when he was only one man, he would certainly let them keep it because they were many. Yahweh rejects this claim because they were practicing idolatry, violence, and adultery.
chapters.34:
## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, Yahweh condemns the leaders of Israel, whom he calls shepherds, and promises that he himself will care for his people, whom he calls his flock.

1. Yahweh condemns the shepherds of Israel for caring for themselves instead of the flock (1–6)
2. Yahweh declares that he is against the shepherds and will rescue his flock from them (7–10)
3. Yahweh will search for his scattered flock, gather it, and shepherd it himself (11–16)
4. Yahweh will judge between the sheep of his flock (17–24)
    1. Yahweh rebukes the strong sheep who mistreat the weak sheep (17–22)
    2. Yahweh will appoint his servant David as the one shepherd over his flock (23–24)
5. Yahweh will make a covenant of peace and give his people safety and plenty (25–31)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Shepherds as rulers

In the ancient Near East, kings and other rulers were often called shepherds, and the people they ruled were called their flock. A good shepherd fed, protected, and searched for his lost animals, so this image shows what Israel’s leaders should have done for the people but failed to do.

### My servant David

David had died long before Ezekiel’s time, so when Yahweh promises to appoint “my servant David” as shepherd and prince over his people (23–24), he means that there will be a future king from David’s family who will rule like David. This is one of many prophecies in the Old Testament concerning the Messiah.

### Covenant of peace

A covenant was a binding agreement between two people or groups of people. Here Yahweh promises an agreement between him and his people that will bring his people peace, which includes safety, prosperity, and well-being in their land.
chapters.35:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is a prophecy against Edom, which Ezekiel calls “Mount Seir.” It sets up a contrast with the next chapter, in which Yahweh promises to restore the mountains of Israel.

1. Yahweh tells Ezekiel to prophesy against Mount Seir (1–2)
2. Yahweh will make Mount Seir a desolation (3–4)
3. Yahweh will punish Edom for its violence against Israel (5–9)
4. Yahweh will punish Edom for claiming Israel’s land and speaking against him (10–13)
5. All Edom will become desolate because it rejoiced over Israel’s desolation (14–15)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Edom and Mount Seir

The Edomites were descendants of Esau, the brother of Jacob, and lived in the region centered around the mountains of Seir, which is the name that Ezekiel uses for Edom. Edom had been hostile to Israel for a long time, and when Babylon destroyed Jerusalem, the Edomites helped the enemy and hoped to take Israel’s land for themselves.

### Punishment that matches the offense

Yahweh repeatedly says that he will do to Edom what Edom did to Israel. Edom shed Israel’s blood, so blood will pursue Edom; Edom rejoiced that Israel’s land was desolate, so Edom’s land will become desolate.
chapters.36:
## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, Yahweh proclaims for the mountains of Israel the opposite of the judgment that he announced against Mount Seir in the previous chapter. He promises to restore the mountains of Israel, and he promises to cleanse his people and bring them back to their land for the sake of his holy name.

1. Yahweh speaks to the mountains of Israel (1–15)
    1. Yahweh will punish the nations, especially Edom, for seizing and mocking Israel’s land (1–7)
    2. Yahweh will make the mountains fruitful and fill them with people again (8–12)
    3. The land will no longer be accused of devouring its people (13–15)
2. Yahweh explains that he scattered Israel because they defiled the land, and that they profaned his name among the nations (16–21)
3. Yahweh will restore Israel for the sake of his holy name (22–32)
    1. Yahweh will gather his people, cleanse them, and give them a new heart and his Spirit (22–28)
    2. Yahweh will make the land abundant, and his people will be ashamed of their former ways (29–32)
4. The rebuilt land will be like the garden of Eden, and the nations will know that Yahweh did it (33–36)
5. Yahweh will make his people as numerous as the flocks brought to Jerusalem for sacrifice (37–38)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Profaning and sanctifying Yahweh’s name

A person’s name represented his reputation. When Israel was exiled, the nations concluded that Yahweh could not protect his own people, so they dishonored Yahweh for that. When Yahweh restores Israel, he will show the nations that he is holy and powerful.

### Uncleanness and cleansing

Israel’s law treated certain bodily conditions, such as menstruation, as making a person ritually unclean, and priests sprinkled water to make people and things ritually clean again. Yahweh uses these images to describe how Israel’s sins defiled themselves and the land and also how he will make his people clean and able to worship him again.
chapters.37:
## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, Yahweh gives Ezekiel a vision and a symbolic action that both show how he will restore Israel. The dry bones that come to life represent the exiles returning to their land, and the two pieces of wood joined into one represent the reunion of the northern and southern kingdoms.

1. Yahweh shows Ezekiel a valley full of dry bones (1–3)
2. Ezekiel prophesies to the bones, and they come to life (4–10)
    1. The bones come together and are covered with sinews, flesh, and skin (4–8)
    2. Breath enters the bodies, and they stand up as a great army (9–10)
3. Yahweh explains that he will bring his people out of their graves and back to their land (11–14)
4. Ezekiel joins two pieces of wood to show that Judah and Joseph will become one (15–20)
5. Yahweh will make Israel one nation under one king, his servant David, and live among them forever (21–28)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Judah and Joseph

After Solomon died, Israel divided into two kingdoms. The southern kingdom was called Judah, and the northern kingdom was called Israel. However, the northern kingdom was also often called Ephraim, after its most prominent tribe, or Joseph, after Ephraim’s ancestor. The two pieces of wood represent these two kingdoms, which Yahweh promises to unite again.

### “My servant David”

David had died long before Ezekiel’s time. When Yahweh says that “my servant David” will be king over his people, he means a future king from David’s family line who will rule as David did. This expected king became referred to as the Messiah.
chapters.38:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter and the next are a prophecy against Gog, a ruler from the far north who will lead a great army against Israel after Yahweh has brought his people back to their land. Yahweh will defeat Gog so that the nations will know that he is Yahweh.

1. Yahweh tells Ezekiel to prophesy against Gog (1–3)
2. Yahweh will bring Gog and his allies from many nations against the restored land of Israel (4–9)
3. Gog will plan to plunder Israel while its people live in safety (10–13)
4. Yahweh will bring Gog against his land to show the nations that he is holy (14–16)
5. Yahweh will judge Gog in his fury (17–23)
    1. Yahweh will shake the land of Israel with a great earthquake (17–20)
    2. Yahweh will destroy Gog’s army with sword, plague, hail, fire, and sulfur (21–23)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Gog and the nations with him

Scholars are not sure who this Gog is. The nations that come with him, such as Meshech, Tubal, Persia, Cush, Put, and Gomer, lived at the far edges of the world as Israel knew it, so the list shows that peoples from every direction will gather against Israel.

### The end of the years

The expressions “after many days” and “in the end of the years” refer to a time in the distant future, after Yahweh has gathered his people from the nations and they are living securely in their land.
chapters.39:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the prophecy against Gog from the previous chapter. It describes Gog’s defeat and its aftermath, and then it turns to Yahweh’s promise to restore Israel.

1. Yahweh will defeat Gog and his army on the mountains of Israel (1–8)
2. The people of Israel will burn Gog’s weapons for seven years (9–10)
3. The people of Israel will bury Gog’s army in the Valley of Hamon Gog to cleanse the land (11–16)
4. Yahweh invites the birds and wild animals to a great sacrificial feast (17–20)
5. Yahweh will show his glory and restore his people (21–29)
    1. The nations will understand that Israel went into exile because of its sin (21–24)
    2. Yahweh will bring his people back and pour out his Spirit on them (25–29)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Cleansing the land

Under the law of Moses, dead bodies made people and places ritually unclean. That is why the people of Israel would spend seven months burying the dead and would appoint men to search the land for any remaining bones.

### Yahweh’s sacrificial feast

In 39:17–20, Yahweh speaks of Gog’s defeated army as a sacrifice and invites birds and wild animals to eat it as guests at his table. The warriors and princes are described as if they were rams, lambs, goats, and bulls offered in sacrifice.
chapters.40:
## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, Ezekiel begins his description of his vision of the restored temple which continues through chapter 48. He describes the outer wall, its gates, the outer courtyard, the inner gates, the inner courtyard, rooms in the courtyards, the altar, and the entryway to the temple building.

1. Yahweh brings Ezekiel to see the temple vision (1–4)
2. The man measures the outer wall and eastern gate (5–16)
3. The man measures the outer court and northern gate (17–27)
4. The man measures the inner court and southern gate (28–49)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The temple complex

In this chapter, God takes Ezekiel in a vision to see a restored temple in the land of Israel. As Ezekiel describes this restored temple, he assumes that his readers already know what temple complexes in his culture were generally like. He simply starts describing what he sees, starting from the outer wall and moving in. The temple complex he describes has an outer and an inner wall. There is an outer courtyard between the two walls and an inner courtyard within the inner wall. Each of these walls has three gatehouses in it, one each on the north, east, and south sides. The gatehouses in the outer wall protrude into the outer courtyard. The gatehouses in the inner wall also protrude into the outer courtyard. See below for a description of each gatehouse. There were rooms around the outer wall and a pavement in front of them. There were some rooms near the gatehouses through the inner wall. Within the inner courtyard, there was an altar and the temple building itself. The temple building was on the far west side of the temple complex, which is why there were no gates on this side.

### The gatehouses

Each gatehouse had the same structures and measurements. There were steps leading to the gateway itself. Behind the gateway, there was a hallway that passed through the rest of the structure. On each side of the hallway were three alcoves with low walls in front of them. For the outer gatehouses, the hallway ended in a porch, which opened onto the outer court. For the inner gatehouses, the porch was in front of the hallway so it too could open onto the outer court. Ezekiel learns the measurements and some of the decorations for all these parts of the gatehouse.

### Ezekiel’s guide

In this chapter, Ezekiel’s guide is called “a man” or “he.” Most scholars think that he is an angel. There are many other stories in this culture about angels who guide a human and show special things to that human. However, Ezekiel does not specify anything about this “man” except that he is bright and shining. Consider how you might refer to this “man” without being too specific.

### Long cubits

In verse 5, Ezekiel states that the man’s measuring stick used long cubits. These cubits were the length of a standard cubit plus one handbreadth. Standard cubits were around 46 centimeters long. A handbreadth was about 8 centimeters. So, these long cubits were around 54 centimeters long. This the length of the cubit that Ezekiel uses throughout the rest of this section. The UST expresses the appropriate measurements in centimeters and meters.
chapters.41:
## Structure and Formatting

5. Ezekiel brings messages of hope (34–48)
    * Jerusalem and the temple restored (40–48)

In this chapter, Ezekiel learns about the measurements, decorations, and one piece of furniture for the temple building itself. He also learns about the courtyard around the temple building and a structure to the west of the temple building.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Long cubits

In 40:5, Ezekiel states that the man’s measuring stick used long cubits. These cubits were the length of a standard cubit plus one handbreadth. Standard cubits were around 46 centimeters long. A handbreadth was about 8 centimeters. So, these long cubits were around 54 centimeters long. This is the length of the cubit that Ezekiel uses throughout this section. The UST expresses the appropriate measurements in centimeters and meters.

### The temple building

The temple building includes two primary rooms, the “nave” (the Holy Place) and the “holy place” (the Most Holy Place). The Holy Place is a rectangle, and the Most Holy Place behind it to the west is a square. The temple building also has a rectangular entryway. There are side chambers whose back walls butt up against the outside wall of the temple building. The temple building sits on a raised platform or foundation. The whole temple building, including the side chambers, is 100 cubits from east to west and 50 cubits from north to south.

### The side chambers

There are three stories of side chambers. It is possible that each story was a single, long chamber that went around the outside of the temple building. It is more likely that each story contained 30 individual rooms that went around the outside of the temple building. There is either a ramp or stairs leading to the higher stories. The higher stories are deeper than the lower stories. This may mean that the temple wall narrowed as it went up. It may mean that the upper stories hung over the lower stories. Scholars are not sure what these side rooms were for. They may have been for storing things.

### The courtyard around the temple building

There was a small courtyard around the temple building. On the north, west, and east sides, there were 20 cubits of space between the edge of the temple building platform and the edges of the courtyard. On the east side of the temple building was the main inner courtyard, which is 100 cubits square according to 40:47.

### The structure to the west

Ezekiel mentions a “structure” on the west side of the temple building, separated by a small courtyard that is 20 cubits wide. This structure has walls that are five cubits thick. Its exterior measurements are 100 cubits from north to south and 80 cubits from east to west. It is uncertain how tall this building was or what its function was. Most likely, its back wall butted up against the outside wall of the temple complex on the west.

### The altar, or table

In 41:22, Ezekiel refers to an “altar,” but his guide then calls it a “table.” Scholars guess that this is the same kind of table that the priests used in the tabernacle and temple to present the special bread to God. In this sense, it is like an altar, since priests use it to present things to God.

### The doors

In 41:23–24, Ezekiel describes the doors that close the entrances into the Holy Place and Most Holy Place. For each entrance, there are two sets of doors. Most likely, one set was at the front of the sill or threshold and the other set was at the back, leaving a small space in between. Each set of doors had two panels, which were connected to the side walls by hinges. In this way, the panels could open by swinging toward the walls. Consider how you might refer to this style of door in your language.
chapters.42:
## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, Ezekiel learns about rooms that are grouped together into two buildings, one to the northwest of the temple building and one to the southwest of the temple building. He learns that these rooms are for the sacred offerings and clothing. Finally, Ezekiel learns the dimensions of the outer wall of the whole temple complex.

1. The man shows Ezekiel the chambers for the priests (1–14)
2. The man measures the outer boundaries of the temple area (15–20)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The chambers

There are two buildings full of chambers, one to the north and one to the south of the structure and courtyard to the west of the temple building. Scholars agree that these buildings are three stories high, and that the highest story’s rooms are smaller than the rooms in the lower stories. Scholars disagree on many other things about how these buildings were constructed. There is a walkway next to each building, but it is not certain which side of the building it is on. There is a wall near the walkway, but it is not certain exactly where it runs. There are “ledges” on each building, but it is not certain exactly what they look like or what their function is. It is clear that these buildings were for the priests to use while they were interacting with holy places and things. When the meaning of a description is uncertain, consider following a major translation in your area or the reading represented by the UST.

### Holy and common

In this chapter, there is a strong distinction between what is holy, or set apart for God, and what is common, or ordinary. Holy and common places, things, and people are not supposed to mix. Both the wall around the temple complex and the two buildings in this chapter help separate what is holy from what is common.
chapters.43:
## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, Ezekiel sees Yahweh return to the temple. Yahweh then speaks to him. He tells Ezekiel about what the Israelites did wrong in the past what he needs to tell them now about this temple. Then, he tells Ezekiel about the altar and the sacrifices required to consecrate it.

1. The glory of Yahweh returns to the temple (1–12)
2. Yahweh gives instructions for the altar (13–17)
3. Yahweh commands the consecration of the altar (18–27)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Yahweh returns

In this chapter, Ezekiel sees Yahweh’s glory arrive at and enter the temple. This is important in the book of Ezekiel because in chapter 10, Yahweh leaves the temple. When Yahweh leaves it is judgment against the Israelites. So, when Yahweh returns, it is repairing the relationship between the Israelites and Yahweh. Ezekiel says that Yahweh’s glory looked like what he had seen previously. These previous visions are in Ezekiel 1 and 8. See those chapters for help in translating terms and ideas in verses 1–5.

### The altar

In verses 13–17, the sacrificial altar for the temple is described. Much of this description is difficult for scholars to understand. There are three important decisions that translators need to make. First, is the altar made out of three sections or just two? It is clear that the altar is made up of square sections that are stacked on top of each other. The higher section is two cubits narrower than the section it sits on. What is not clear is whether there are two or three of these sections. The UST models an altar with three sections. Second, how many gutters are there on this altar? It is clear that there is a gutter around the base of the altar. This gutter collects the blood from the animals. This may be the only gutter, or there may be a second gutter at the edge of the highest section of the altar. The UST models an altar with two gutters. Third, verse 17 indicates that one of the sections is 14 cubits on each side. Which section is this? It may be the highest section or the middle section. The UST models an altar which has a 14-cubit square highest section. The altar also has a square area on the top for burning the sacrifices and horns at the four corner of this square area.
chapters.44:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the vision of the new temple that began in chapter 40. After Yahweh’s glory has returned to the temple, Yahweh gives Ezekiel rules about who may enter the temple and how those who serve there must live.

1. Yahweh establishes rules for the temple entrance and worship (1–9)
2. Yahweh assigns duties to the Levites and priests (10–16)
3. Yahweh gives instructions for the priests’ conduct and service (17–31)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Levites and priests

All priests were Levites, but not all Levites were priests. Here Yahweh says that the Levites who led Israel to worship idols may guard the gates and slaughter the people’s sacrifices but may not serve at the altar, while only the priests descended from Zadok may come near to Yahweh to serve him.

### Holy and common

Many of the rules in this chapter keep what is holy separate from what is common or unclean, such as the linen clothes the priests must leave in the holy rooms before they go out to the people. Yahweh says the priests must teach the people to tell the difference between these things (see verse 23).
chapters.45:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the vision of the new temple that began in chapter 40. Yahweh describes how the land around the temple is to be divided, and then gives instructions about honest measures, offerings, and festivals.

1. Yahweh sets apart a holy portion of the land for the temple and priests (1–8)
2. Yahweh commands honest weights and measures (9–12)
3. Yahweh establishes offerings and sacrifices for the people (13–25)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The holy contribution

The “contribution” or “offering” in verses 1–7 is a strip of land that the Israelites were to set apart for Yahweh when they divided the land among the tribes. It contained the sanctuary and the land for the priests and Levites, and the city and the prince’s land lay beside it.

### The prince

The “prince” is the ruler of Israel in this vision. He received land of his own so that he would not take land from the people, and he was responsible to provide the sacrifices for the festivals on behalf of all Israel.
chapters.46:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues Yahweh’s regulations for worship in the new temple and then resumes Ezekiel’s guided tour of the temple courtyards.

1. Yahweh establishes regulations for Sabbath and daily offerings (1–15)
2. Yahweh gives instructions concerning the prince’s inheritance (16–18)
3. Yahweh shows the places for preparing the offerings (19–24)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The prince

The prince is the ruler of Israel in Ezekiel’s vision of the restored nation. He has a special place in the worship of the temple and provides offerings for the people, but he is not a priest, so the priests offer his sacrifices for him.

### The year of liberty

Every 50th year, called the year of liberty or the year of Jubilee, land that had been given or sold to someone outside the family was returned to its original family. This is why a gift of land to a servant would return to the prince.
chapters.47:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues Ezekiel’s vision of the new temple. It describes a river that flows out from the temple and gives life to the land, and then Yahweh sets the borders of the land that the tribes of Israel will inherit.

1. Yahweh reveals the river flowing from the temple and bringing life (1–12)
2. Yahweh establishes the boundaries of the promised land (13–20)
3. Yahweh commands the division of the land among the tribes (21–23)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### “the eastern sea”

The river flows east into the Arabah and into “the sea” in verse 8, which is called “the eastern sea” in verse 18. This is the Dead Sea, a lake so salty that no fish can live in it. When the river makes the salt water fresh, the passage speaks of the waters being “healed” as it becomes full of fish.

### Inheritance of the land

Yahweh gives the land to the 12 tribes as a permanent possession, as he promised their ancestors. The tribe of Joseph receives two shares, one for each of the tribes descended from his sons Ephraim and Manasseh. Foreigners who live among the Israelites and raise families there also receive an inheritance.
chapters.48:
## Structure and Formatting

This chapter concludes Ezekiel’s vision of the new temple and the restored land. Yahweh divides the land among the tribes of Israel, describes the holy portion in the center of the land, and names the gates of the city.

1. The portions for seven tribes north of the holy portion (1–7)
2. The holy portion of the land (8–22)
    1. The portion set apart for Yahweh, with the sanctuary in its midst (8–9)
    2. The portion for the priests (10–12)
    3. The portion for the Levites (13–14)
    4. The common land for the city (15–20)
    5. The land for the prince (21–22)
3. The portions for five tribes south of the holy portion (23–29)
4. The gates of the city and its new name (30–35)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The tribal portions

Each tribe receives a strip of land that runs across the whole country from the eastern border to the Mediterranean Sea, and the tribes are listed in order from north to south. This is different from the way the land was divided in the time of Joshua.

### The holy contribution

The “contribution” is the land that the Israelites were to set apart for Yahweh between the portions of Judah and Benjamin. It is a square that contains the sanctuary, the land for the priests and the Levites, and the city, and the land of the prince lies on its east and west sides.

### The name of the city

The city receives the name “Yahweh Is There.” This shows that Yahweh, whose glory Ezekiel saw leave the temple and the city in 10:18–19 and 11:22–23, will live among his people again.
